name: Recommendation Letters
title: Recommendation Letters
answer: AI can help a counselor or teacher draft the structure of a recommendation letter or suggest ways to describe a student's strengths, but the specific stories and details that make a letter meaningful must come from the writer. Because a letter carries the writer's name and reputation, and admissions readers can often recognize generic writing, the substance has to come from the person who knows the student. Writers also need to read every draft for bias and accuracy, since AI tools can repeat stereotypes found in the text they learned from.

sections.body: Counselors and teachers write many recommendation letters each fall, often under heavy time pressure, and AI can take some of the load off the drafting stage. It can propose a structure or offer ways to phrase a student's strengths when the writer is facing a blank page. The problem it solves is time pressure at a moment when letters matter a great deal to students. But the worth of a letter does not come from its shape, it comes from the specific examples that only the writer knows. A letter that sounds like every other letter does little for the student, so AI is useful for scaffolding and not for substance.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice the writer begins with whatever the tool offers, a structure or suggested ways to describe a student's strengths, and then does the real work of the letter. Before anything is entered into a tool that is not covered by a signed agreement, names and personal details are removed. The writer then adds the specific stories and details that make a letter meaningful, the material only they can supply. The text does not lay out separate steps by grade band, so the same sequence applies wherever letters are written, in a counseling office or a classroom. The drafting help targets the fall crunch, while the judgment about what to say stays with the writer.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or finding for this idea, and it carries no evidence label. What it offers instead is the observation that admissions readers can often recognize generic letters and that a letter sounding like every other letter does little for the student. That claim comes from practice and professional experience rather than from research cited in the book. Readers should treat the idea as a working practice, not as a finding backed by data.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A recommendation letter carries the writer's name and reputation, so accountability for what it says cannot be handed to a tool. AI drafts can repeat stereotypes found in the text they learned from, including in how they describe different students, so the writer should read every draft for fairness and accuracy. Removing names and personal details before using any tool not covered by a signed agreement is a condition of using the tool at all. The decisions about what a student is really like, which examples to include, and whether a draft is fair all stay with the person who knows the student. Each student deserves a letter that reflects who they really are.
